articles.title: Wardle Resident Contributes to New Poetry Trail Focusing on Recovery
articles.excerpt: John Bailey, a Wardle resident in recovery from substance use, has collaborated on a poetry and audio trail designed to promote healing and reflection. The project features contributions from local individuals and is set to launch in September.
articles.content_html:
A Wardle resident has played a significant role in the creation of a new poetry and audio walking trail aimed at promoting recovery from substance use. John Bailey, who has been in recovery for just over a year, is one of 15 participants from Turning Point's Rochdale and Oldham Active Recovery service, known as ROAR, who collaborated with poet Phil Davenport on the project.

The trail, titled 'If You Could Speak to the World', features seven spoken poetry pieces and is a self-guided walking route that begins in Oldham town centre and leads into Northern Roots. The audio recordings are complemented by music composed by Sophie Cooper and performed by Milnrow Band. Bailey, a former bar and restaurant manager, participated in outdoor sessions at Northern Roots during the spring and early summer, where he and other participants, aged from their 20s to their 70s, created poetry inspired by the landscape and recorded sounds for the trail.

Bailey expressed that a key aspect of his recovery has been embracing new opportunities. As an English literature graduate, he found the project particularly appealing. He described a technique used during the sessions where participants reflected on gratitude, sadness, and historical perceptions of their surroundings, leading to the creation of 'found poems' that resonated deeply with the group.

The shortest version of the walking trail spans two miles, encompassing all seven poetry locations, while longer routes extend up to six miles. Maps will be available from the Northern Roots Welcome Building and online starting in September. Guided walks are scheduled for September and October to officially launch the audio trail, which was commissioned by the visual arts organisation Portraits of Recovery and funded through Transport for Greater Manchester's Wheels and Walks programme.
